utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Veton Surroi. I have an oral application to make that you may be aware of. This witness was previously indicated as a viva voce witness, a live witness. We'd indicated to the Defence counsel and Trial Chamber via e-mail I think late last week that we intended to use Rule 92 ter to introduce his written ICTY statement and his transcript, in addition to having some live evidence from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any opposition to that, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There is no opposition to that, Your Honour. But perhaps before the witness comes in we could address an issue that we say arises in the light of your decision yesterday on the use of time. We asked for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's obviously not going to apply strictly in this case. I think that's fairly obvious. And I suspect that little need be said on the matter. If you are endeavouring to complete cross-examination in the course of today, now, obviously you cannot be tied to that right at the outset. But I gather that the plan is for Mr. Hannis to keep his examination to a minimum, to give you the rest of the day, and hopefully you will, in return, endeavour to complete your cross-examination within that time. If that's an accurate description of the scene, then we don't regard that as firmly binding, but we hope that we can achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour. But I have to indicate, I think yesterday I said I was going to try and do it in 15 minutes. Based on reviewing my notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And now it's turned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I think it's going to take me longer. I understand the longer I take, the more likely it is that I'm going to require the witness to have to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have him in, please. Oh, sorry, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you can have him come in, but I just wanted to say that I want to have a time to speak to yesterday's order, and I'm willing to do it at your convenience. You just tell me when and I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what respect, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the order carries with it an assumption which is obviously not valid, and that is there are only two parties here, the Prosecution and the Defence, and that's not true. There are seven parties here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it does -- it doesn't, Mr. Ackerman, carry that assumption at all, and it clearly indicates that, as situations arise, then the matter will need to be dealt with on an individual basis. But that's not a matter for debate at this stage or in the immediate future. We will consider any application that's made on a reasonable basis, as the order makes clear. But the order itself is a reasonable assessment of the overall situation, having regard to all that's happened in the course of the trial so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly agree that it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may learn more from our experience as we go along. We've tried to set these as guidelines that we shall try to follow, and in so far as that's impossible in the interests of justice, then we will modify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make certain any objections I may have I'll have an opportunity to put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, indeed. The final part of the order makes that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's have Mr. Surroi, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honour, his evidence will pertain to paragraphs 25 to 32 and 77 through 100 of the indictment. His written statement is Exhibit P2361, his statement of 27 August 2001. His transcript from Milosevic is P2362, on the 18th and 19th of April, 2002. There were two exhibits in that transcript; Milosevic Exhibit 101 is our Exhibit P696, and Milosevic Exhibit 102 is our Exhibit P712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 696 is what document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the UN Security Council report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the other one is a Bertelsmann document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I can give you page references to the transcript, if you need them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not at the moment, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Surroi. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth in your evidence by reading aloud the document now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which language do you propose to use in the course of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Albanian, my mother language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the first counsel to examine you will be Mr. Hannis on behalf of the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Veton Surroi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, I want to go through a list of things regarding your personal background, and at the end I'll ask you to confirm whether I've got it correct or not. You are a Kosovo Albanian, the son of a Yugoslav diplomat. You lived some years of your youth in Bolivia, South America and Mexico. You have a Bachelor's degree in philosophy and letters. And you are a journalist and a publisher by profession. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're currently a member of the Kosovo assembly or parliament?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand you're also part of the Kosovo delegation engaged in some international negotiations about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before today, sir, did you have a chance to review your written statement to the ICTY that was dated 27 August 2001?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you also have a chance to review the transcript of your testimony in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, which was given on the 18th and 19th of April, 2002?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And having done that, are you satisfied that both of those are true and they accurately reflect your evidence or your statements, to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you confirm to this Court that that evidence is what you would give under oath today if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender P2361 and 2362 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. And with the accompanying exhibits, or are you going to deal with them separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I would like to tender them at this time as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's P696 and 712.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect for Mr. Veton Surroi, I wanted to point out a problem I've noticed by following the transcript of today's testimony. In the Serbian, this was the second page of the second day of the cross-examination of Mr. Surroi by Slobodan Milosevic, on the 19th of April in 2002. In the English, this is page 3474. 3474, yes. Something interesting happened, and I believe this will require a decision on the part of the Chamber. There was a discussion between Judge May, rather an intervention by Judge May, when Slobodan Milosevic asked a question of the witness concerning the NATO attacks on Yugoslavia. Judge May interrupted at that point and said that the witness was not supposed to give his opinion of that. He said this would be just the witness's opinion and this is up to the Chamber to decide. And then Judge May said, "You are the only one asking him for his opinion, and his opinion is no longer relevant." You will agree, I believe, that both in the statement and in the examination-in-chief as well as the cross-examination and the opening remarks of Mr. Hannis today, there is often mention of Mr. Surroi's opinions. Therefore, I'm puzzled. We are interested in the opinion of Mr. Surroi, but whether we should stick only to that or only to the things that he personally experienced, heard or saw. And I believe this requires some instruction on your part so that we could be able to choose the direction of our questioning. I apologise. I didn't want to take up too much of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The best guidance I can give you, Mr. Fila, is in relation to the very point that you raise here, the question of whether NATO bombing was a criminal act or not. Now, Judge May was of the view, as you've seen, that that was a matter that the Trial Chamber in that case would have to determine. It may or may not be a matter that has to be determined by the Trial Chamber in this trial. That yet remains to be seen, whether it's an issue. But even if it is an issue for this Trial Chamber to determine, the opinion of Mr. Surroi on the point - and I mean no disrespect to him on this - is immaterial as far as this Trial Chamber is concerned. He's not presented in a capacity in which he could express an opinion on that matter that would have an influence on our judgement in this case. Now, if there are other matters of that nature which arise, you will need to raise them in cross-examination and we will make an assessment of them, if you feel there is an opinion there you want to clarify the point -- the position of. But so far as this one is concerned, his view on the matter is not of relevance to our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You warned me last time that I was a bit too hasty on occasion, and I believe this happened today as well. I didn't mean only Mr. Surroi's opinion of the NATO pact. It means nothing to me. But, in principle, his statement and his answers during the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination contains his opinion on many things, and often. Therefore, my question is: Are we going to deal here with Mr. Surroi's opinion about all the issues that we are to touch upon, or are we going to hear him only on things that he personally experienced, as someone who can testify as to the crime base? I hope I made myself a bit clearer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, he will testify on matters, obviously, that Mr. Hannis will now raise with him. This transcript is part of the record of the trial. You will have an opportunity to make submissions, in due course, that there are parts of this that we should give absolutely no weight to or have regard to for various reasons, including that it is an opinion of someone either not qualified to give an opinion or possibly on a matter which is for the Court to resolve and not for him to express a view on. These are arguments that we will deal with in due course. If we were a jury sitting in this case, we might hesitate about allowing that evidence to come in at all. But I think you can trust us to exercise the correct judgement in due course, in light of your submissions at the end of the case. But if you want to pursue any of them in particular, if you do it in cross-examination, we will address it as and when it arises. Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is what I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, in the interests of time today, I'm going to try to keep my direct examination short. Your written evidence in the form of the transcript and your prior statement are in evidence, and the Court has that before it. I want to go directly to 1989 in Kosovo. In your statement, we see a reference to the revocation of the autonomy of Kosovo in 1989 and the introduction of the so-called special measures. Were you aware of the circumstances that surrounded the vote taken in the Kosovo assembly at that time regarding the revocation of autonomy?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. As a journalist at that time - I was working for a newspaper Rilindja - but also as an ordinary citizen, I saw with my own eyes that the Kosova assembly was surrounded by the police forces, including APCs. And before the vote, I heard that there had been pressure on the delegates of the Kosova assembly, pressure had been exercised also in the meeting, the meeting for this revocation of Kosovo's autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, have you ever interviewed a member of that assembly who was a party to the decision who has told you that he made a decision only because of pressure either from weapons outside the building or pre-decision pressure exerted by some other influence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke with members who voted against that decision, with the few that voted against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Have you ever spoken with someone who voted for it and says he did so only because of that pressure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any irregularities in connection with that vote?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. I had the photograph of the voting in my office, and you could see clearly from the photograph that the person who was not a member of the assembly was voting there. His name was Mehmet Ajeti. Later on, he was a guard in -- sorry, not a guard but director of the prison of Mitrovica. And on the basis of that photograph and on the basis of evidence that he had, my friend Bajram Kelmendi had brought this case against the revocation of the autonomy of Kosova before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the vote, as I understand it, was taken by a show of hands, a raising of hands?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. It was an open ballot with a show of hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this individual that you've named, is it Mr. Ajeti?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he a member of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the assembly of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What organisation did he belong to at that time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm sure he was not a member of the assembly of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with the imposition of special measures subsequent to that time, what effect did that have on everyday life for you and other Kosovo Albanians? How did things change?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was clear that the repressive policy would continue. At that period, as was shown already, there was a practice that was called the isolation practice, which meant kidnapping people and keeping them in prison, without trying them in a regular trial, for a period of 60 days. As a journalist at that time, I discovered this in the Croatian and Slovenian media and denounced the practice of arresting people like this, arresting individuals and keeping them in prison without due process. After these people were released from prison, I interviewed some of these people and they told me about the torture and beating that occurred in the prison. These were people who, in one way or another, were organised or participated in various protests against the revocation of the autonomy of Kosova. In these prisons, they had this practice of "hot rabbit" they called it, where the welcoming of the prisoners was like this: There was a line of policemen that beat up the prisoners when they passed along this line. It's like running the gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: During the time between 1989 and 1999, was there an effect on education for Kosovo Albanians as a result of these changes?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After 1990, the first victim was education, so to speak. At that time the Serbian regime wanted all people who worked in the public sector to sign a piece of paper where they swore that they would work for the Republic of Serbia. It was a kind of an oath. The citizens and the employees who were Albanians, most of them refused to sign these statements, and as a result, they were expelled from all public activities. The first to suffer was education, but also of course the whole Albanian education system which was deinstitutionalised, and for a long time pupils in high schools and secondary schools and students in the faculties were not allowed to enter the premises of their schools. There was this physical division between Albanian students and pupils and Serb students and pupils, even when they were allowed to go to these schools. My daughter, for example, when she went to school for the first day, she was divided, she was in a separate place in the school, which was the place where the Albanian pupils, and there was no heating in the Albanian part of the schools but there was heating in the Serb part of the school. This is a discriminatory policy that was followed in education at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of the so-called education agreement or the San Egidio agreement of 1996? And, Your Honours, could we bring up Exhibit P715, 715, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after the agreement was signed, the next day, I met the person who signed the agreement, the late Fehmi Agani, who had signed it on behalf of the Kosova party, and there was Ambassador Maslovaric --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement was brokered by monsignor --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the aim of this agreement was for the Albanian students to return to Albanian school and to improve the situation for Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I guess the interpreter missed a couple of names that you indicated. Could you tell us again the name of the ambassador who was involved?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: His name was Maslovaric, if I'm not mistaken. He was Serbia's -- the Serbian ambassador, or at the time ambassador of the FRJ in Vatican, while the broker was Monsignor Paglia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic eventually sign that agreement?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Chairman Rugova had authorised Professor Agani to act on behalf of the Kosovars, knowing that Mr. Milosevic would be behind this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was the freedom of press affected in Kosovo during this time between 1989 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From 1990, from July 1990, measures were taken, repressive measures were taken against the Prishtina radio and television, so the Albanian -- Kosovar Albanians did not have their own public TV. There were other repressive measures in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Perhaps Mr. Surroi made a mistake but he said that Fehmi Agani signed the agreement, but this is not the agreement that I have before me. I believe there is another agreement here that we are talking about. Perhaps this should be corrected in the transcript. This was obviously an error or a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can we have that clarified, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the English version of that exhibit on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Surroi, I don't know if you can see that on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] I cannot. Now I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this is an English translation but if we can scroll to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, I think the gentleman I think what I said was that Dr. Agani was authorised to negotiate and evidently Dr. Rugova signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, we were speaking of freedom of the press. I don't know if you had finished your answer before.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't finish. So the repressive measures of the Serbian regime in 1990 had done so that there was only one Albanian publishing house in Kosova but that was administered by the Serbs as well, and they controlled the printing and the distributing of everything. So after Rilindja was closed they were controlling every other newspaper and magazine in Albanian. So from 1990 to 1996, there were restrictions, severe restrictions, in expressing yourself in the Albanian language in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two other questions regarding the atmosphere and the changes between 1989 and 1999. Was there any change in the nature of the police treatment of Kosovo Albanian civilians during that time period?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: With revocation of autonomy, the police and the MUP, which until that time was under the pressure of the Belgrade authorities, had now -- had now become completely under the control of the Ministry of the Interior, the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, and it had become a plenipotentiary power above all legal restrictions. It was easy at that time, the easiest thing to kill an Albanian of any age, and during all that time, there was no repercussion with regard to these issues. There was this -- an open permission to use violence, physical violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One last matter in this regard, if you can help us out with a linguistic matter that came up, I think early in the trial at page 1118 to 1120 of our transcript. Mr. Lukic was asking another witness about the Albanian word "Siptar." I understand that's the Albanian word for Kosovo Albanian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, the correct pronunciation is "Shqiptar".

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I need help with my pronunciation. I understand that in Serbian that there are two related words that deal with that, "Albanac," which means Albanian, and "Siptar." Do you understand the difference and can you explain that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The correct use of the Serbian language, the word to use in that language for Albanians is "Albanac." In the period starting from the 1950s and 1960s, the word "Shiftar" took a negative connotation, and it was used again in the 1970s in a derogatory sense. The explanation we heard at the time was that we -- there needed to be a distinction between Albanians in Kosovo and Albanians in Albania, but the real cultural context of the use of this word "Shiftar" was describing a second-hand citizen. When I discussed this with Mr. Milosevic, we discussed this and I said this was used daily. If a family, Albanian family in Belgrade, would want to buy something in Belgrade, they would have to ask for a Siptar and not a worker to do that job for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, the word "Siptar" is translated by the interpreters here as Albanian, not Kosovar Albanian. Can you -- Mr. Hannis's question was on the basis, that "Siptar" had a particular meaning, Kosovo Albanian. That's not been my understanding so far. Can you clarify that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The real context of the word "Siptar" in its cultural form is to make a distinction between Albanian from Albania and Kosovar Albanians initially, but then with the time in the 1970s and the 1980s, it was used in a derogatory form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me, though, give you the particular example here. When a witness from Kosovo who is Albanian is asked, "What is your ethnicity," the witness will say "Siptar," and the interpreter will say Albanian. Now, if that was an Albanian from Tirana and not an Albanian from Kosovo, and that person was asked, "What is your ethnicity," what would the answer be in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the interpreter would translate it the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. And in Serb it would be "Albanac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that it's because the Serb uses the Albanian word but sometimes somehow or other it's perceived to have a derogatory sense. I think I've got that message. But I was just trying to clarify the distinction between a Kosovo Albanian and an Albanian Albanian, and so far as language is concerned, there isn't one. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, then is it fair to say that the word "Siptar" standing alone doesn't necessarily have a negative or derogatory connotation. It depends on who is using it, towards whom, and in what context?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to go to page 3 of your English statement and page 4 in the B/C/S, with reference to the group called G5 and a meeting that G5 had on the 15th of May, 1998, with Mr. Milosevic. First of all, could you tell us briefly who made up the G5 and what was that group? For what purpose was it created?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The G5 in fact was just a reduction of the number of 15 members who were elected members of the negotiation group for Kosova. However, when Rugova decided to meet Mr. Milosevic, he then invited us, four other of us, to join him in this meeting with Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade. So from 15 members, this number reduced to 5. So it was Mr. Rugova, Fehmi Agani, Pajazit Nushi, Mahmut Bakalli, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you describe in some detail in your statement and in your testimony about that meeting with Mr. Milosevic and his personal adviser. I know one topic that you addressed with Mr. Milosevic was the killing of the Adem Jashari family that had happened I think around the 5th of March 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court briefly what that event was about and in what context you brought it up with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, are you saying that the statement is deficient in relation to this? Because it's gone into in some detail and it's also gone into in the transcript, and we have got a lot of information about it. Is this really useful use of your time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I thought just -- it may not be the best use of my time but I thought just briefly to put into context the following questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we have the context. I've got an impression that this might be more grandstanding than productive examination, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not trying to grandstand, I promise you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll move on to something else because it is fairly well detailed in your statement. You did indicate in your statement that you challenged Mr. Milosevic about that, if he thought indeed there had not been any improper conduct by his police that there was no reason why he should not invite an international, impartial forensics team to investigate what had happened. I believe you indicated he said he would check into that. As far as you know, was that ever done in connection with the Jashari family killing?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement you describe how in 1999, in February, you took part in the negotiations that took place in Rambouillet and Paris, France, in February and March. Who was that organised by?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was organised by the member countries of the contact group. Formally it was organised by the British and French governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you tell us that Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic were both present at times during those negotiations. Were you able to determine their respective roles in that process?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Sainovic, for quite a long period of the negotiations, was the political leader of the Belgrade delegation, though the direct negotiations from a legal point of view, the person in charge was Mr. Markovic. Mr. Milutinovic was coming every now and then from Belgrade to participate in this commitment, but there were negotiations with Mr. Milosevic as well, but Milosevic was not participating there. And whenever there was need for consultations, then Mr. Sainovic would fly to Belgrade to consult Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to page 11 of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S. You mention meetings that your colleague Baton Haxhiu and Mahmut Bakalli had with representatives of the security service of Serbia, including Jovica Stanisic. Do you recall now approximately when those meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, because I learned about it later. Therefore, I don't remember exactly when it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if it was before the Rambouillet talks?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Of course, yes. It was before violence escalated in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It must be two years before or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will have additional evidence about that from Mr. Haxhiu, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, I want to ask you finally about after the time when the NATO bombing started - page 12 of the English of your statement, page 13 of the B/C/S - you indicated that on the 24th of March individuals described as police broke into the offices of your newspaper, ransacked the office and killed the guard, Mr. Ramadani. What was your source of information about how that had been perpetrated and that it was police who had done it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were two neighbours who had seen this scene, neighbours in the editorial office and they had described this event later. The following day, the director of Koha Ditore went there but he was not permitted to enter the building. He had seen traces of blood on the staircase up to the street where his body had been dragged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, this is the sort of hearsay that's very difficult to give any credence to. Two neighbours, unnamed, no information about what they saw. I mean, are you anticipating we'll have any regard to this sort of hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm hoping that together with this hearsay and other information you hear before the case is over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as long as you're not relying on this on its own and you feel you've supplemented it in any way. Because all we know -- we have advanced our knowledge to the extent that we know it's two neighbours but we don't know any more. And I am going to go back to another issue that you've dealt with, but if you want to do any more on this, first of all, then I'll go back in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of those neighbours or are you not willing to?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I withdraw that question, Your Honour. I have no more questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other matter then, Mr. Surroi, on which I certainly would be interested, if you could help us further, is the source of your knowledge that Mr. Sainovic, first of all, was the political leader of the Belgrade delegation at Rambouillet and Paris and that he was in fact travelling to get instructions from Mr. Milosevic, and also your source of knowledge that -- of the role that Mr. Milutinovic had and what exactly that role was. Now, can you tell us more specifically about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On 22nd of May, 1998, when we held this round of talks in Prishtina, the first and last round of talks between Belgrade and Prishtina, that delegation was headed by Mr. Sainovic. In the room where this meeting was held, that is, in the offices of LDK, near that room, Ambassador Chris Hill, the then American envoy for the Kosova issue, was sitting in the next room. He was ambassador to Skopje. I consulted Mr. Hill on the relevance of Mr. Sainovic, and he told me that Mr. Sainovic was the closest man to Mr. Milosevic regarding Kosova issue. I received a message from Mr. Hill and conveyed it to Mr. Sainovic, and the message was that Mr. Hill was in the room next door, and that if Mr. Sainovic wanted to consult him on any issues, he was ready to meet him. This was the impression I had in Rambouillet as well. And on that occasion, I consulted again Mr. Hill. Wherever we asked the question what was the relevance of the negotiations team of Belgrade, Mr. Chris Hill always replied that Mr. Sainovic was the most trusted man of Mr. Milosevic. As for Mr. Milutinovic, we have not seen him directly involved in negotiations. However, in the palace, in the last stages of the negotiations, I happened to be there during that time when the European, American and Russian mediators were making their last efforts to convince the Belgrade delegation to sign the Rambouillet agreement. To my recollection, in the room where Mr. Milutinovic was, Jonathan Ovitz [phoen], a member of the American delegation, entered that room to convey him the last message, that is, that with this part of negotiations, the Rambouillet process was over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will follow the order of the indictment, and I have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Eugene O'Sullivan and I represent Mr. Milan Milutinovic. Good afternoon. I have to ask for your indulgence to a certain extent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, would you kindly speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You are fluent in English. I have documents that are in the English language only; I regret that I don't have them in Albanian. Could we work with the English language documents this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibits are already in e-court, and I have hard copies for distribution to the Chamber, the Prosecution and for Mr. Surroi. I believe the names of the individuals who should receive the packages are on the cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I trust they are all the same and not customised, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Only the names are different. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to Rambouillet for a few minutes. The Rambouillet conference was held in the Rambouillet Castle, which is located south of Paris; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you said it was organised by the contact group. And the six countries which formed the contact group were the US, the UK, France, the Russian Federation, Germany and Italy; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the contact group foreign ministers at the relevant time were Madeleine Albright, the US Secretary of State; Robin Cook, the British Foreign Secretary; Hebert Vedrine, the French Foreign Minister; Joschke Fischer, the German Foreign Minister; and Lamberto Dini, the Italian Foreign Minister. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Igor Ivanov of the Russian Federation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I believe you said the co-chairs were Mr. Vedrine and Mr. Cook; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there were three contact group negotiators, and they were Ambassador Chris Hill of the US, Ambassador Boris Majorski of Russia, and Ambassador Wolfgang Petritsch, who was an Austrian but represented the EU; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And each one of the contact group negotiators had a team of experts or assistants working with them, and by that I mean Mr. Majorski had his people, Ambassador Petritsch had his, and Mr. Hill had his assistants.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And one of the people assisting Ambassador Hill was Jim O'Brien from the US State Department.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at the time of Rambouillet, Germany held the Presidency of the EU; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up Exhibit 1D16. The hard copy is tab 1, and I can represent to the Court and to you, Mr. Surroi, that at tab 1 is a calendar of the month of February 1999. I have it in front of you just for ease of reference, perhaps to orient ourselves more easily with the dates. It's correct, is it not, that the Rambouillet conference started on Saturday, the 6th of February, and finished on Tuesday, the 23rd of February? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And initially the Rambouillet conference was scheduled for one week with the possibility of extending it into a second week; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] ... initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't ...

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] There wasn't such a strict deadline in that sense, but it was, orientationally, a two-week conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on the 14th of February, on that Sunday, the foreign ministers met at Rambouillet and in fact extended the meeting until the 20th, the following Saturday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at the end of the second week, on the 20th of February, the foreign ministers, the contact group, met once again at Rambouillet and extended it to the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And your delegation was composed of 16 members, I believe.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were all ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And some of your members -- some members of that delegation were from the late Mr. Rugova's LDK party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And some members were from Rexhep Qosja's party.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: For the record, the spelling of the name is R-e-x-h-e-p, Q-o-s-j-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Qosja's party was known as the United Democratic Movement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that members -- certain members of Mr. Qosja's party were disgruntled former LDK members?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And some of his members also had close links with the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Also in your delegation were members of the KLA --

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- including Hasim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then I think would you agree that there were independents such as yourself and your fellow journalist, Mr. Blerim Shala?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Thaqi was selected head of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would it be accurate to say that some of the members of your delegation had never had any personal contact with other members before coming to Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Some of you had not even met before Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, aside from the members of your delegation, the 16, you also had assistants from certain consultants or experts such as Ambassador Morten Abramovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He's a US lawyer and former US State Department --

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, he was an ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also had a Professor Marc Weller?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: For the record, that's M-a-r-c, W-e-l-l-e-r.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And he's at the Centre for International Studies at Cambridge University; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And prior to Rambouillet, he had been at times giving legal advice to the government of the Republic of Kosovo, I believe.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: He could have been. I did not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One more person I'd like to ask you about who was not formally in the group of 16 is a man named Dukagjin Gorani, who was a journalist at your newspaper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. He came as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to Sunday, the 14th of February. That's the day that Madeleine Albright came to Rambouillet; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on that day she chaired a meeting between members of your delegation and members of the FRY Serb delegation.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That was the only time that the members of the two delegations actually met face to face; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would it be fair to characterise that meeting as a protocol meeting, where each side had a chance to express their views, show goodwill, without getting into the substance of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. The aim was to create this rapprochement because there was no movement towards this process of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, on the same day, the 14th, prior to this joint meeting, Mrs. Albright had also met separately with your delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And one of the things she told you is that, if the agreement was not signed because of the Albanians, America and the international community would abandon you.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: She also told you that if the agreement was not signed because of the Serbs, the Serbs would be bombed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It probably wasn't on that day, but in one of those days, she did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that, except for the one meeting with Ms. Albright as chair, the two delegations didn't meet at Rambouillet. But the contact group negotiators and the experts would meet with the members of each delegation separately; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And changes to documents that were tabled by the contact group, changes could occur either through a process of agreement between the delegations or if the contact group was persuaded by one side that a change was necessary.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The changes were carried out only when the three negotiators agreed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the 6th of February, the first day, an initial draft of the Rambouillet agreement was presented to the two delegations by the contact group negotiators; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 1D18; e-court page 418. For those of us working in hard copy, Mr. Surroi, that's tab number 3. Have you found tab 3? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a point of, perhaps, procedure and I have a suggestion for dealing with this. Exhibit 1D18 is, in fact, the book I'm holding in my hand, which is over 400 pages. It's a book entitled, "The Crisis in Kosovo," by Professor Marc Weller. And I know that your order in July on exhibits or procedures would be that only those portions of a book that were used in court would be admitted, and so I'm only proposing that, by way of identification, I could point to the page range of Exhibit 1D18 for admission. In other words, what you're looking at at tab 3 in hard copy, the range is page 418 to 425 in e-court. And that's the full text of this draft agreement which is dated 6 February 1999, document number 5 in the Weller book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just let me check one thing before we determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is this book one of the stand-alone documents that the Prosecution tendered as the source of this agreement? Or is it another volume?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it was a different volume, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's quite important here to confine ourselves to as few documents as possible. And if there can be -- if there can be Prosecution agreement, not necessarily at this minute, that this is an accurate record of the first draft, then we can confine our consideration as we go along to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe the Prosecution has offered the first draft. They've offered the draft of the agreement of the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you're doing or propose that we do, Mr. O'Sullivan, is appropriate, and we will note that our consideration of this particular exhibit is confined to these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, the document you have in front of you, which is Exhibit 1D18, e-court pages 418 to 425, is the initial draft which was given to the parties by the contact group negotiators on the 6th of February. It's correct to say, is it not, just looking at the beginning of this document, that this draft contains the political components of the Rambouillet agreement? In other words, annex 1 is the constitution of Kosovo; annex 3 is the elections; annex 6 refers to the ombudsman. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, on the 16th of February, both your delegation and the FRY Serb delegation presented the contact group negotiators with comprehensive comments and responses to this initial draft; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We submitted responses all the time. We were involved in the negotiating process from the first day, so we made comments and responses from the first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, is there or are there other annexes that are not published here, or at that time did the proposal only contain these three annexes with non-consecutive numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My understanding is that these were the annexes which were tabled on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At that stage. With the possibility of others being interposed, I assume. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I understand that you say you made proposals throughout. My question was a little more specific, sir. On the 16th of February, that is the Tuesday of the second week, that's the -- at that day, the contact group received both from your delegation and the Serb delegation, comprehensive comments and responses to this particular draft or the work that had been going on since the 6th.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I cannot know what Belgrade proposed at the time, but I know that we had the obligation to make assessments and comments and also to receive comments from the foreign ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could go to same exhibit, 1D18, e-court page 429, 430, Mr. Surroi, that is tab number 4 in the hard copy. Again from the Weller book. It's document 11. It's a press briefing by the spokesman for the contact group negotiators on the 16th, and this may refresh your recollection, sir. It's the first paragraph. In the middle of that first paragraph, left-hand column, the spokesman Mr. Phil Reeker says: "As of this morning, the negotiators have been presented with comprehensive comments and responses to the contact group draft interim agreement from both the Kosovar Albanian and FRY Serbian delegations." Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Probably does. I don't see where that is, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's document 11. It's tab 4.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Tab 4, but I don't see that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Should be page 432 of the -- left-hand column at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Press briefing. What I just read to you is what Phil Reeker said on behalf of the contact group. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So in your Prosecution interview, which is Exhibit P2361, when you say that the Serbian delegation never responded during the Rambouillet process, that's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Responded to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll read it to you. You said in your OTP statement, page 8: "Another indication of their lack of seriousness was that in the first two weeks, the international negotiators had asked both delegations for responses to the initial draft documents. The Serb delegation never provided any responses." I'm putting it to you that that's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The form -- when it was said, no. [Interpretation] The issue is that we did not have any respective responses in the period of the first week. There was no response in the first week. In the second week that you mentioned, there was a position that was taken by the Serbian party, but that was a position that would not lead to -- towards the negotiating process. The Belgrade delegation insisted on signing the principles of the contact group.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we have here the spokesman for the contact group saying that indeed on the 16th, the FRY Serbian delegation had given comprehensive comments and responses. You don't dispute that, do you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I cannot speak here in the name of the spokesperson or what he thought the case was, but I'm -- if I speak on behalf of my delegation, we did not see any progress on the part of the Serbian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Again, in Exhibit 1D18, page 431 to 438, that's the e-court page range, that's tab 5 in the hard copy, again from the book produced by Marc Weller. It's the Interim Agreement for Peace and Self-Government in Kosovo, second draft, 18 February 1999. Sir, this is the second draft which was produced on the 18th, two days after both delegations had given comprehensive responses to the initial draft, and I don't want to go into great detail with you on this document, we can read it at our leisure, but if you just flip through this document you can see that there are -- there is a more comprehensive document than the initial draft. There is a chapter 1 on principles; a chapter 2 on confidence-building measures; chapter 1 on the constitution, chapter 3 on the elections; chapter 4 on economic issues; chapter 4A humanitarian assistance, reconstruction and economic development; and the same chapter 6 we saw before, the ombudsman. Now, this is the document the contact group produced, is it not, based on the exchange of views and responses from both delegations on the 18th of February?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This is a document proposed by the mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct. But based on the work of both delegations; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I don't know on the basis of what, but I think this was presented as such. I cannot assess or evaluate the work that the Serbian delegation did. I can only speak here about the work we did with the mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very well. When your delegation received this second draft, the members who were negotiating the political components were so annoyed they wanted to quit, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: They said they would not touch this document at all?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: That was an emotional reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Still, Your Honour, in Exhibit 1D18 the Weller book page range 441, 442, it's tab 6 of the hard copy. We have here the Kosova delegation statement on new proposal for a settlement dated 18 February 1999. Mr. Surroi, this is your delegation's reaction or statement that was issued after you received the second draft from the contact group on the 18th of February. I'd like to look at certain portions of it with you. For example, the first paragraph, I'm looking at the top right-hand column first paragraph, it says: "The Kosova delegation has studied the revised proposals relating to a political settlement put forward by the contact group. This is a substantively new draft introduced after Kosova has negotiated constructively on the basis of the initial proposal put forward by the contact group. The Kosova -- the delegation of Kosova returns this document to the contact group as it is unacceptable for consideration at this late stage. In fact, it represents a breach of faith by the contact group. The reasons for this attitude are as follows." Now, you considered the second draft that we've been looking at as procedurally and substantially unacceptable, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, as you can see from this letter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And your reason -- the process, as you've told us, it was not face-to-face meetings but proximity talks shuttling between the delegations by the contact group negotiators; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I put it to you before that the process was either on the basis of agreement by both delegations or if the contact group were persuaded by arguments put forward by one of the parties, those proposals would be integrated into the Rambouillet agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. I said it earlier that these changes could be done only by the mediators, the three mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And yet you receive this document on the 18th, the contact group proposal, and your reaction is to return it to the contact group and reject it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We are speaking about a context of the negotiating process where we had finished, because this was done in two different speeds, if I may say so. We had our own speed in doing things. We had reached a certain stage. We had gone through a negotiation process where we had made our concessions, the necessary concessions, and the possible concessions. The changes in the quality of the document caused this disgruntlement in our delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the process, shall we? We've seen that on the 16th of February, the contact group negotiators received the comprehensive views and comments of the FRY delegation. Now, the reason that there were no face-to-face talks isn't because of the FRY delegation. In fact, didn't they propose on numerous occasions to have face-to-face talks with your delegation. You said no and the contact group supported your position? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. We asked for no meetings before the first phase of the negotiations is over. In other words, before this document issue was cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And isn't it also correct that at the very beginning of the Rambouillet process, the first few days, the FRY Serb delegation had asked as a sign of goodwill, I would say, that both they and your delegation sign the nonnegotiable principles which had been the basis for the Rambouillet agreement, your delegation refused and the contact group supported your position?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear, because the nonnegotiable principles were approved by the very fact that they refused to come. Mr. Cook wanted to go to Belgrade. Instead of flying to Prishtina, he flew to Skopje because he was not allowed to fly to Prishtina. Before the Rambouillet conference, we were given these nonnegotiable principles and we accepted them and we expected the Serb side, as a sign of goodwill, to stop the fighting. We filed this request but unfortunately it was not taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, it would be helpful if you could clarify the reference there to the principles being approved by the very fact that they refused to come.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the translation. The nonnegotiable principles were adopted by the sole fact of participation. We accepted that we would enter a negotiating process based on the nonnegotiable principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That makes sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: To follow up on that, Mr. Surroi, the same document you have in front of you at tab 6, which is e-court 1D18 page range 441, 442, the Kosova delegation statement. I'm looking at the second paragraph where you make reference -- your delegation makes reference to these principles and I'll read it to you. "The delegation of Kosova notes that the nonnegotiable principles proposed by the contact group envisage an interim agreement with a mechanism for a final settlement after an interim period of three years. On this basis, the delegation of Kosova has accepted to come to Rambouillet." That's what you were saying, I believe?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. Not only this. There were other nonnegotiable principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And wasn't one of those nonnegotiable principles the territorial integrity of FRY?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: That was one of the biggest problems for the delegation. But the fact of the matter is that we were negotiating based on the present realities and on the assumption that we would have an open process by which there would not be a prejudged outcome of these negotiations, so the territorial integrity on the one side would not hurt our aspiration for independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Wasn't your biggest complaint about the second draft agreement we looked at on the 18th the fact that the word "sovereignty" had been included in this second draft, "sovereignty of FRY as a territorial integrity"?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's precisely what it says in your statement, your delegation statement at the seventh paragraph, one from the bottom of the right-hand column, where it says that the first point relates to the insertion of the word "sovereignty" into the preamble of the annex. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In other words, the word "sovereignty" appears for the first time in the Rambouillet drafts and that was the main objection your delegation had or one of the main objections you had. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We've had many -- you know, this is a negotiating process. We have had so many objections. I suppose everybody had objections. I could not recollect all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And if we turn to the next page of this same document, the Kosova delegation statement, your proposal there is that you're insisting on the insertion of reference to a referendum on the final status of Kosovo. You say that must be included in the Rambouillet agreement so that a referendum can be held after the three year interim period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, certainly, the objection you raised here, and the insertion of reference to a referendum would be contrary to the territorial integrity of the FRY, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. A process of getting a part does not mean that it affects sovereignty. It just accepts the creation of new sovereignties.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Moving ahead to Friday, the 19th, you were aware that on that day, at the end of the second week, Mr. Thaqi, the head of your delegation, travelled to the city of Ljubljana, Slovenia, to meet with Adem Demaqi; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Demaqi was a senior figure in the KLA, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At that time, I don't know what he really was, but he was a political figure, an emblematic figure linked to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on the same day, the 19th of February, isn't it correct that members of your delegation were allowed to leave the Rambouillet castle to meet with General Wesley Clark who tried to persuade the Kosovars to sign the agreement?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Some of the members of the delegation went and met Mr. Clark, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's move to Saturday, the 20th. That's the -- that was the second deadline, what was supposed to be the second deadline of the process, and the contact group foreign ministers are there and they summon a meeting with representatives of both delegations. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the four members of your delegation who appeared before the contact group meeting were you, Mr. Thaqi, Mr. Qosja, and Mr. Rugova; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, in this room there were the six foreign ministers, the three negotiators, the staff assistants, interpreters; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there was a bit like a trial, wasn't it, perhaps reminiscent of how things feel right now, right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Prior to that meeting, you'd been briefed by the contact group negotiators and asked to answer a very specific question, perhaps with a "yes" or "no", a question whether you could accept the Rambouillet political settlement as it existed based on this 18th of February draft; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, whether we would accept it fundamentally, with the possibility of making some technical corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that during this meeting with your delegation, at one point, the Italian Foreign Minister, Mr. Dini, asked Thaqi whether you could accept the document with no reference to a referendum and Mr. Thaqi said you could not?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Wasn't it at that point that Mr. Dini turned to Mrs. Albright and made a gesture as if to say, "See, I told you so"?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At that point the foreign ministers and negotiators were shocked, if not surprised, by Mr. Thaqi's position; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yeah, they continued to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But shortly thereafter, the meeting was adjourned because of the confusion created by Thaqi's response to Ambassador Dini?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. Mr. Fischer began to ask questions, Joschka Fischer.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But there was clearly not a "yes" that the contact group foreign ministers and others were expecting from your delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't complete. It was a "yes" that needed time of negotiations, further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was a "yes, but".

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A "but war," which was nonnegotiable you were told by Robin Cook, I believe, the question of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. We insisted on the referendum. We fought for that until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, after you left the room, you know that the representatives of the Serb FRY delegation came in - and you may or may not know this - but they gave their support to this political document. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was a question of including both documents, the political and military one. We had been asked the same question. It was not only the question -- the political side but also the military side, which was problematic to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me suggest this to you: On the 20th of February, the military or security implementation part of the agreement wasn't there. That came later. On the 20th we were talking about the political framework. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We had talked about security issues as well at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But it wasn't in this document that you were being asked to comment on.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the next day, the 21st of February, the Sunday, members of your delegation have a working lunch with Mrs. Albright; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, four members of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we get to that, do you accept, Mr. Surroi, that on the 20th, the FRY delegation met the contact group in the same way as you did and they said that they found the political agreement acceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I cannot speak on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, on the 21st, Sunday, again, I believe it was you, Mr. Thaqi, Mr. Qosja and Mr. Rugova were having a working lunch with Mrs. Albright; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And also present at that occasion is Jamie Rubin, her spokesman from the State Department.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: During the discussions over lunch with Mrs. Albright, your group stated that you wanted the Rambouillet agreement to include explicit reference to a referendum.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A referendum conducted by the people of Kosovo on their right to statehood after the three-year period.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the word "referendum" doesn't -- did not and does not appear anywhere in the Rambouillet agreement, does it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now we can call up Prosecution Exhibit P474, which is the Rambouillet agreement of the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would this be a suitable time to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- because we will need to shortly. We will interrupt now. Mr. Surroi, you'll be shown where to wait while we have our break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, we were talking about the working lunch you had with Mrs. Albright on Sunday, the 21st, at which time the representatives of your delegation told her that you wanted explicit reference to the referendum by the people of Kosovo in the Rambouillet agreement, and you also had confirmed to me that the word "referendum" doesn't appear in the final Rambouillet agreement, doesn't appear in any of the drafts or the final. That's where we left off. I had asked that Prosecution Exhibit P474 be brought up, and you will find -- at page 25 in e-court. You will find that at tab 9 in the hard copy. Tab 9 of the hard copy is page 25 of e-court. And I want to direct your attention to chapter 8, "Amendment Comprehensive Assessment and Final Clauses." Now, before I ask my question, I want to put this in context in time. What you're looking at is the last page or the final clauses of what was the final Rambouillet agreement, the one that was dated 23 February 1999. That's the final version; I can represent that to you. What we have been looking at together were earlier versions of the 6th and the 18th. So I have moved ahead now to the final version. And it's paragraph 3 that I wanted to look at with you. Chapter 8, Article 1, paragraph 3: "Three years after the entry into force of this agreement, an international meeting shall be convened to determine a mechanism for a final settlement for Kosovo on the basis of the will of the people, opinions of relevant authorities, each party's efforts regarding the implementation of this agreement and the Helsinki final act, and to undertake a comprehensive assessment of the implementation of this agreement, and to consider proposals by any party for additional measures." I read this to you because of the phrase "the will of the people." Now, at one point during your lunch on the 21st of February, a couple of days before this clause actually appeared in the Rambouillet agreement, you asked Jamie Rubin whether Mrs. Albright could provide the Kosovar delegation with a side letter giving assurances that the USA understood the phrase "expressed will of the people," to mean the right of the Kosovo people to hold a referendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Rubin spoke to Mrs. Albright and she agreed to prepare a letter like that for you.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This was a conversation that I had with Mr. Rubin and Mrs. Albright.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the draft letter that Mrs. Albright prepared concerning these assurances, you showed it to Ambassador Petritsch and you asked Ambassador Petritsch if the EU could provide your delegation a similar letter; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I first showed it to our delegation, then to Mr. Petritsch, because I thought that the same thing should go for the European Union as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D18, that's the Marc Weller book once again; e-court page 499; tab 7 in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
