utterances.text: There, Mr. Surroi, Professor Weller has put a document called "Draft for Chapter 8, Article 1.3, 22 February 1999, 0525 hours, and Proposed Draft Side Letter." Now, the first paragraph of this document is the clause from the Rambouillet agreement that I read to you that includes the words "expressed will of the people," and below that is the text of the letter, which reads: "This letter confirms the formulation attached above, proposed for Chapter 8, Article 1.3, of the Interim Framework Agreement. We will regard this proposal or any other formulation of that article that may be agreed at Rambouillet as confirming a right of the people of Kosovo to hold a referendum on the final status of Kosovo after three years." Now, you say you requested of Ambassador Petritsch to see whether the EU could provide you with a similar letter, and the response you got was that such a letter was not possible. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You were told that the EU, Russia, the FRY were all opposed to including reference to a referendum in the Rambouillet agreement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I would like to emphasise here that Madeleine Albright's letter was withdrawn officially because our delegation, by that time, had not fulfilled the obligations of acceptance. Therefore, this letter was legally not valid at the last stage of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in this process where you're dealing with Mrs. Albright and Ambassador Petritsch, my question was: It was made clear to you that, as far as the international community was concerned, inclusion of a referendum by the people of Kosovo was nonnegotiable; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I think Mr. Petritsch's formulation was that he was not in a possibility to produce such a letter. It is a fact that at that time there were 12 states of the European Union that needed to consult each other on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can refresh your memory. You were interviewed by a Brook Lapping television production company. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have the transcript of that interview and I can just read from it or I can show you the document. Perhaps we can just do it first by reading from what you told Brook Lapping, which was used in the production of the BBC document, "The Fall of Milosevic." And I'm quoting from the transcript which we received from the Office of the Prosecutor. You said this: "The problem was we insisted on the use of the term 'referendum' and on the right that the eventual referendum automatically gave us statehood and independence after a three-year period. This was nonnegotiable as far as the international community was concerned. They said, 'We cannot include that' because it meant giving us independence automatically. It would not be accepted neither by Belgrade nor by the international community in general." Now, that's what you told Brook Lapping, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Well, "nonnegotiable" is a metaphorical expression at this stage because it became negotiable. And the will of the people was included in the -- in the document. There was strong opposition to the use of words -- of the word "referendum," clearly so. And even the letter that we had received by Secretary Albright was withdrawn from circulation afterwards because of non-fulfilment of obligations, because we had not basically signed the agreement at the right hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. But it was withdrawn because of the reaction, in part, because of the EU and the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] No, no. We had a deadline and the deadline was to sign the agreement that day. We failed and therefore the letter was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this period, very short period, between the 20th and the 23rd, those extra days that were added on to the conference, in light of this letter that was withdrawn, in light of the EU reaction to opposing "referendum" appearing in the agreement or side letters to your delegation, the debates within our delegation became quite heated, didn't they, on how to deal with the referendum issue; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at one point, it's quite -- it's correct, is it not, that the head of your delegation, Mr. Thaqi, was an opposed to the agreement and was actually working against not signing it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And it was on the last day of the conference, on the 23rd of February, that last day, in the morning, that's the day that Ambassador Hill brought you and the other delegation, the FRY delegation, the final text of the Rambouillet agreement, which included the political and the implementation annexes, the document that ultimately became the Rambouillet agreement.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We had copies of the documents of that time. This was the text that we accepted to sign, by accepting at the same time that this document did not become a subject of negotiations again.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go through the 23rd of February with you briefly. I have suggested to you that you received the text from Ambassador Hill on the morning of the 23rd, and the deadline was approximately 3.00 or 4.00 that afternoon to accept or not; correct? The last day.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, but that was the document we had been negotiating all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. So we agree.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that day, in the morning of the 23rd, your delegation couldn't agree on what to do, and in fact not only was Mr. Thaqi opposed to it, but other members of your delegation were also becoming more and more opposed to the signing of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that by mid-day, lunchtime, your delegation had stopped working, that you'd gone for a big lunch and you were sitting around having desserts when Chris Hill walked in?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Ambassador Hill was quite upset, wasn't he, because no progress was being made?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And isn't it then that you came up with the idea of drafting a letter from the Kosovar delegation to Mrs. Albright?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Not only to Mrs. Albright but to negotiators as well, including the contact group.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But your idea -- my question was specific to your idea of drafting a letter from your delegation to Mrs. Albright. That was one of the ideas you came up with; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This was the idea of the entire contact group.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the letter -- you wrote a letter or a letter was prepared in your conference room. It was typed by Mr. Gorani, your translator, in the presence of the Albanian delegation, Ambassador Hill, Jim O'Brien and other people from the American delegation; correct? And the letter was to Mrs. Albright.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I will tell you the details because it is quite an important part, what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you agree or disagree with what I just stated?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Well, I agree partly, but the letter was not intended for Mrs. Albright alone. It was intended for the whole contact group.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, this letter was typed up by Mr. Gorani on his computer, and while he was typing it, weren't people from the US delegation blocking Mr. Thaqi's access to the computer, like in a basketball game?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a moment when Mr. Thaqi wanted to change the words that we agreed to use earlier. And in an atmosphere, a heated atmosphere like that, Mr. Thaqi was prevented from repeating his positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And he was physically blocked, like in a basketball game, by members of the US delegation; isn't a correct description?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Since there were people there, it could look so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to e-court 1D18. That's, again, the book of Professor Marc Weller. E-court page 467, that's tab 8 in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On that page, in the left-hand column, in the middle, Professor Weller has included a document entitled, "Letter from the Delegation of Kosovo to US Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, 23 February 1999." Now, that's the letter that Mr. Gorani prepared and the one that you signed and the one that was given to Mrs. Albright; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the second paragraph which begins: "We want to convey to you our understanding on two points. First, we acknowledge your view that the agreement allows and does not preclude a referendum in Kosova which will determine the will of the people in Kosova and which will be conveyed to the international meeting to be convened to determine a mechanism for a final settlement for Kosova as called for in Article 1, paragraph 3, of chapter 8." Now, this letter to Mrs. Albright essentially contains the same assurances that she was giving you from her letter, but you're giving it back to her; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] We were trying to fish.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you knew and she knew that her letter had been vetoed by the EU, by Russia, by the international community; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] I don't think it's correct at all. I don't think it was vetoed at any point. I think it was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the letter that we have in front of us, the one from your delegation to Secretary Albright, never became public, did it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] It might have. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It was never shown to the Serb delegation, was it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] It probably appeared in the newspapers. I wouldn't doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But this is a side letter addressed personally to Mrs. Albright, not to the contact group; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what would your view be of the legitimacy of a side letter between the FRY delegation, a non-disclosed letter that said there would never be a referendum of the people of Kosovo and territorial integrity would never change? How would you feel about that as a participant in this negotiation process?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] I wouldn't feel entirely happy, but there's not much we could do about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Surroi, I have a few questions for you. But, first of all, let me tell you good afternoon and let me introduce myself. I'm Toma Fila, a lawyer representing Nikola Sainovic. I would like to start with some changes in your statement. You have your statement before you. This was taken by Fred Abrahams, who was also a witness before this Tribunal on the 28th of August. On page 8 of the Serbian text, and on page 7, paragraph 3, of the English version - and I'm going to read it to you - you stated this: "The meeting with the Serbian delegation was held on the premises of the Democratic Alliance in Pristina," and you say, "the Serbian delegation, headed by Prime Minister Ratko Markovic, included Nikola Sainovic, Mr. Oric, and so on and so forth. Do you stand by your statement that the delegation was headed by Ratko Markovic, which is what you stated?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not Prime Minister, he was Deputy Prime Minister. I think Mr. Markovic was not Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He was not the head of the delegation -- was he the head of the delegation or not?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It has been entered in the record. Just nodding your head will not do. Throughout your statement, you provide your opinion as to why they came, and I wouldn't go into that. But you also say that you went to see Chris Hill occasionally during the meeting and that they thought that you went there for your instructions. However, the important thing is that nowhere in the statement you stated that Sainovic played any important role, save for being the head of the delegation. Why are you saying today that you spoke with Christopher Hill about him? You never said it before. You never said it on the examination-in-chief. Maybe your memory was fresher at the time.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that at the time you claimed that Markovic was the head of the delegation, that he headed the delegation, but you never mentioned Sainovic as playing any role, and that Chris Hill informed you about that? This is not part of your statement that you provided then. Was your memory fresher at the time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. It's simply that nobody asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Nobody asked you about that today either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I direct counsel to page 8 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I asked a question earlier today, Mr. Fila, specifically about the role -- about the source of information about the role of Mr. Sainovic at the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know you did, but I'm trying to elicit an explanation as to why he didn't say that in his statement that he provided in 2001. This is my question, as very simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's given you the answer that nobody asked him. But Mr. Hannis wants to help you further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I want to direct counsel to page 8 and 9 of the English where there is some reference in his written statement regarding speaking to Mr. Hill about Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you're referring to. We don't have it, that's for sure. Would you please be so kind as to read this, Mr. Hannis, because I don't have it in my version of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, if you have page 8 of the English version of the statement, the final paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's the last two paragraphs under the topic heading "Rambouillet Conference" and right before the next paragraph heading "Other Negotiations," in English. I believe it starts on page 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. We were talking at cross-purposes then. You're talking about Rambouillet, Mr. Hannis, and I myself am talking about Pristina. I'm talking about Pristina, not about Rambouillet at all. And I was provided with an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In Pristina, Markovic wrote down your proposals and that's where you left it off; is that correct? Very well, then. Before that -- we will come to Rambouillet later. Before that, you went to see Milosevic together with Mr. Rugova on Holbrooke's proposal.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to observe a pause between question and answer for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There is Mr. Rugova on the one hand, the six of you, and on the other hand we have Milosevic. Did this tell you something, that there was nobody else there with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was plenipotentiary in Serbia, so our conversation was with this person who was all-powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well, then. You say that Mr. Agani mentioned the agreement that was signed by Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic regarding the Egidio, and this is where the statement ends. Do you know what happened next with this Egidio thing, or would you like me to give you some documents?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In the implementation phase of the San Egidio agreement, the Albanological Institute was set up and two or three colleges of Prishtina University were to be opened in Albanian. The faculty of philosophy and then the technical faculty was returned to the Albanian professors and students. But, in fact, this agreement remained then to that point because of the further developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You're aware of the fact that the European Union provided 4 million ecu, that Serbs added something to that, that buildings started being built, but that Rambouillet put that process to a halt.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, it was not interrupted by Rambouillet. In the beginning it was procrastinated, because one or two years after the agreement, only then it was -- the implementation phase began. That meant that Mr. Milosevic was trying to procrastinate the process. And I told you that only one or two colleges were opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit 1, which is on e-court. 2D1 is the number of the document. This is the agreement on the implementation which was signed in 1998. You have it in Serbian and in English, but there is also an Albanian version, if you need it. But since you speak English, you won't need it. You will see who the signatories of this document are, as soon as you have it on your screen. This is the Albanian version for you to peruse. There is also an English version that has been provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Sir, this proves what I was saying, that the procrastination was deliberate on the part of Mr. Milosevic, because the agreement was signed in 1996, while the implementation started in 1998, when we started talking with Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade. At that time, in the mountains of Decani, there were about 5.000 refugees who were displaced from their homes and were going towards Albania. So the context we are talking about is almost surrealistic. It's surrealistic to speak about a faculty or university when there are these interethnic problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The essence of the matter is something that I'm going to show you. It can be seen on the document that it was signed by your representatives and the Serbian representatives in Pristina on the 23rd of March, 1998. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was absolutely clear, yes. There was a will.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I want to show two more documents, 2D2, which show how the implementation of the agreement went. We have this document in both Serbian and English but we don't have it in Albanian. But you speak English, so you won't need it, will you? As you can see, this is a document that shows the implementation of the agreement and the amount -- first we want to see 2D2, the Exhibit 2D2. I'm sorry, I'm not very well-versed in this technology. Well, now we have it. You can see from this document that this was not implemented only in letter but that it was really implemented, and you can see the involvement of the European Union. You can see the amount of money that was at stake, and on the next page, you can see -- Can you move up a little, please? Can we go to page 2 of the English version, please? This is still page number 1. Here you can see that the European Union participated with over 4 million ecu and that Serbia participated with 266.000 ecu, and you can see that Serbia fulfilled its commitment and that this was a law, as you've told us.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: If I can say something here, it's only the European Union that wanted to contribute something here. There was nothing else. At that time, one destroyed village was more important than this. So to reconstruct that village cost more than this amount here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is not my purpose to debate this with you. What I am trying to say is that the Serbian side was a signatory and that this was launched. That's why I'm asking for this document to be admitted into evidence. And let's now move on to Rambouillet. First of all, let's divide Rambouillet into two parts, Rambouillet and Paris. I was not there, but I know it lasted for two weeks. Earlier today, you told us that Christopher Hill told you something about the role of Nikola Sainovic, and if I understood you well, neither in Rambouillet nor in Paris you spoke to him or were seated next to him. So you personally do not have any direct knowledge. The source of your information is what Ambassador Hill told you; am I right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Other diplomats as well, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What transpires from your testimony and from your statement is this: You said that, from experience, you knew that nothing could be started in Serbia without Milosevic's approval, and this was your explanation for the fact that Nikola Sainovic, during negotiations, told Chris Hill, which was conveyed to you later on, that Sainovic had to go back to Belgrade for consultations. And that's what Hill told you, that Sainovic had to go back to Belgrade for consultations. Do you adhere by that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you said that Thaqi made the most of that opportunity and went for consultations in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The essence of my question is this: Why did you not say this in your statement in the same way you've said it now? I did not understand you properly because our languages are not the same. You said that Sainovic was politically the head of the delegation, but that the real head of the delegation was Markovic. This is what you said. What does that mean? You spoke about that for the most part. Since you're a philosopher, you will remember the famous words. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I was thinking that because we had the experience of Prishtina, I understood Mr. Markovic's role as a constitutionalist, as a legal expert, who dealt with drafts, while the representation of political interests and the contacts with Belgrade and Milosevic personally, I thought that Mr. Sainovic was going to do that and was doing that. I based this on the fact that Mr. Sainovic was trusted, a politically trusted person of Mr. Milosevic on the Kosova issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is what Hill told you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: But this was also an impression that you could get from the media as well and from everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the last thing I want to ask you is this: At the Milosevic trial, Mr. Nice asked you this - and this is page 3406, line 24 - and you confirmed that Sainovic was one of the representatives of the Serbian side. He asked you whether he left at one point. You said he did, and that was all. You did not say at the moment that he played a more important role, which you're saying now, and Mr. Nice did put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Nice did not ask me why Mr. Sainovic went there, and I think I explained that in my statement or testimony, but I will repeat it here: It was Mr. Hill's obligation, because he was a mediator, he had to tell us that Mr. Sainovic was travelling. This was outside the rules of the Rambouillet agreement, and negotiations, because the agreement said that there would not be any travelling. So Mr. Hill explained to us that he would go with Mr. Sainovic to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have all that. I'm just asking you why you didn't mention a more important role that Sainovic played at the time when you were testifying at the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please just bear with me for a moment? I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do have some questions, and I hope I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic. I'm one of the attorneys representing Mr. Sreten Lukic here today, and I will have just a few questions for you to clarify some matters. First I'd like to talk about to get somethings in context from the testimony that you offered. I'd like to ask you, first of all, about the establishment of the parallel shadow government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you a moment, Mr. Ivetic, in view of the way the time is going, just to clarify something. It may not be possible, Mr. Hannis, but if it were possible, then we would be happy to see the return of Mr. -- who did we start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dashi, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had anticipated that -- when Mr. O'Sullivan ended a little earlier than I anticipated, we made an inquiry. Mr. Dashi is not at the hotel. I know we told him to come back Wednesday. We are trying to locate him, so we might have him here before we finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thanks very much. I'm sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I should indicate to Mr. Hannis that I should have about 15 or 20 questions so he knows what time period we've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mr. Surroi. I wanted to ask you about the time period of 1990 that you're talking about, and I wanted to confirm with you: Isn't it true that around this same time period in 1990, a parallel shadow government was set up by Ibrahim Rugova's party, along with the so-called National People's Movement, to counter the actual official Serbian state government in Kosovo/Metohija, and that this shadow government consisted of Bujar Bukoshi as Prime Minister, and was based in Stuttgart, Germany, where he resided. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This was created later, in 1991, and it was created by the coordinating council of the political parties in Kosova and also by Mr. Rugova, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it accurate to state, then, that in approximately early 1992, this shadow government, this Bukoshi shadow government, established several cabinets, including a Ministry of Defence and a General Staff to coordinate the armed activities of their cause?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Maybe they existed as a name, but in realistic terms, Bukoshi's government, for quite sometime, was based in a motel, a very small motel, and that small motel wouldn't be room enough for a single ministry, let alone other things like staff and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, in your role as a journalist covering events in Kosovo/Metohija, and as a member of various political delegations, do you have knowledge of the fact that the Bukoshi government entered into an agreement with the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Albania, Safet Zhulali, to train and recruit armed fighters for their cause from Kosovo and to train them in the Republic of Albania? I refer to the agreement between Safet Zhulali on the one hand and Hajzer Hajzeri, the Defence Minister of the Bukoshi government, and also Mr. Anton Kolaj, the vice-president of Rugova's LDK.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't hear of this agreement. I don't even know of its nature now. I read about it post festum, after the NATO airstrikes, but I don't have a firsthand knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to move on to the relations between -- strike that. Did you have occasion to hear of this armed wing of the Rugova and Bukoshi camp being coined as the armed forces of the Republic of Kosova, "Forcat e Armatosura te Republikes se Kosoves"? And I apologise for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This is later, maybe autumn 1998. Perhaps earlier than that but it is definitely 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Closer to 1998, I agree. Can we agree to refer to them as FARC, for the sake of --

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it correct that at the time that FARC entered the scene in Kosovo/Metohija, the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, the KLA/UCK had already begun armed attacks against the state institutions of the Republic of Serbia and the federal Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And isn't it also correct that these two armed groups, the FARC on the one hand and the KLA on the other hand, that they began to enter into conflict with one another over strategy and as to who was going to lead the fight for the independence of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I don't have deeper, more profound knowledge on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall a meeting in January of 1998 in Pristina that you attended along with Mr. Rugova, Mr. Thaqi and others in which Richard Gelbard, the Ambassador from the United States, wherein he condemned the activities of the UCK/KLA and labelled them as terrorists?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It seems to me that Mr. Gelbard did not address us in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But do you recall any tensions arising from that meeting on the hand of the LDK faction on the one hand and those that were moving towards supporting the UCK/KLA on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It is quite natural that there were tensions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you also aware of the assassinations of the FARC Minister of Defence, Ahmet Krasniqi, in September of 1998 in Tirana and also of FARC founder Azem Hajdari that were attributed to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Of course I know about the killing of Colonel Ahmet Krasniqi. I know that at that time, even in the capacity of Kosova delegation, we asked for this to be clarified, for the perpetrator to be identified. What I didn't know is that Azem Hajdari was the founder of FARC, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One of the founders of FARC.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I haven't heard that he was a founder of FARC.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Are you familiar with an event in September of 1998, in the Cicavice area, when several Kosovo Albanian politicians aligned with Mr. Rugova's faction were touring the area when they were arrested and threatened by the KLA's so-called police force and were threatened with a hit list that was produced of Kosovo Albanian politicians whom the KLA was targeting for assassination?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this was widely known in Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At the time, I publicly asked for these people to be released, though it was absolutely unacceptable to use violence within internal political relations in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just one more question relating to the relationships between the FARC and the UCK. Isn't it true that after the NATO forces took over -- after KFOR took over control of the territory of Kosovo/Metohija, that another one of FARC's commanders, Tahir Zemaj and his two sons, were killed in circumstances where, again, the UCK was blamed for this action?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Zemaj, I think, was killed two years ago. I'm not sure. The circumstances of that killing, of his killing and his son's killing, are not clarified yet. The KLA on the other hand was immobilised and transformed in 1999. For the sake of the terminology used here, I would like to explain this: That pursuant to a proposal by Ahmet Krasniqi, all the armed forces fighting for the liberation of Kosova were supposed to be called UCK, or Kosovo Liberation Army. So for some time, there was no distinction between FARC and UCK. It was only used as UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but there was infighting as to who was going to be the overall leader of that combined military faction; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There could have been, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to just clarify a couple of points from your direct examination. You testified as to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and I wanted to confirm with you the fact that, prior to 1990, the Ministry of Internal Affairs that operated on the territory of the province of Kosovo/Metohija was, in fact, a stand-alone provincial ministry that was not at all tied to the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Belgrade. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Interior as it was called at that time, the SUP of Kosova, hierarchially was not linked to the Secretariat of Serbia. It was not subordinated to it. It was linked to the federation, to the Secretariat of the Interior at the federal level, as other Secretariats. I would like to tell you that the system of internal affairs in Yugoslavia, even the entrance of other MUP forces from other areas could have been carried out by prior decision of the SUP of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the SUP of Kosova at that time -- well, strike that. Let me move on. You mentioned also in your direct examination some evidence relating to allegations of what transpired in prisons, and I want to ask you about both the time period prior to 1990 and the time period subsequent thereto, are you aware of the fact that the prisons in Kosovo/Metohija and, indeed, throughout the Republic of Serbia which fall under the Ministry of Justice are not staffed by employees of the Ministry of Interior, that is to say, policemen? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: When I described the issue of isolation, I wanted, actually, to point out that the guards were not police. They were separate guards, staff of the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: But it does not reflect the reality. When you have isolations of persons who have not been tried there, all the distinctions and all the divisions between internal segments are broken. So a judge and police can become the same thing, and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. One moment. Thank you, Mr. Surroi, for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an few questions on redirect for you, Mr. Surroi. Mr. O'Sullivan was asking you about Exhibit 1D18, which I think is tab 4 in the hard copy. It's a press briefing by Mr. Reeker. You talked about the fact that submissions had been received from both parties, from your delegation and from the Serbian delegation. However, if you go to the top of the right-hand column, there is a question from a reporter about, "Can you tell us the progress of this past weekend of negotiations?" Mr. Reeker says they received some things. And then the question is: "When you say handed over, does this mean that the Serbian delegation is now giving written documents?" Answer: "Yes. That was, if I can make clear, they have both now presented written comments." Now, in your statement, you indicated for two weeks -- you indicated for two weeks there had been no response. Mr. O'Sullivan pointed this out to you and got you to concede, Well, it appears that by the 16th, 10 or 11 days after the conference began, they had submitted something. But from this colloquy it seems that it was only recently that they submitted something. Is that consistent with your memory of the events?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. As I said, we were continuously negotiating. It was a one-sided negotiation because we never received a response before, prior to this, from the Serb delegation. The technique of the negotiation was that we would be responding to the same document to the negotiators; the negotiators would pick up the comments from both sides and would switch -- and would propose to the other side what the -- what one side had suggested, and would draw on issues which they think might be a compromise and offer them as compromise. And this is how our political group had functioned. But for quite a number of days, we never received anything from the negotiators, because those were the ones who were supposed to bring us papers from the Serb delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it your understanding of the process that the comments that you had been submitting were being forwarded to the Serbian delegation?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] I think they were, and this is certainly the feedback we had received from the mediators and their legal assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that there had been no sign of proposals to amend the original draft prior to the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] To my memory, there wasn't anything significant to remember. And when the deadline approached, that was the moment when we received the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the 16th of February would have been after Mrs. Albright had sat and met with your delegation and with the Serb delegation? As I understand, she met with you on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] She met with us on St. Valentine's, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if she met with the Serb delegation that same day?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. We met altogether, not only with ourselves but we met altogether as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked a question about when Mr. Sainovic requested and got permission to leave. Was Mr. Thaqi's departure before or after that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] It was after the departure. We had been informed by Ambassador Hill of Mr. Sainovic's departure, and we were then abruptly informed after some hours by Mr. Thaqi that he had the intention to go as well and that he had asked the mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you -- I think you said, in connection with that, that that was contrary to the initial terms of the negotiating process; that no one was supposed to leave. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The agreement was that only the translators and whoever was -- whoever did not have a sleeping dwelling in the castle would leave but not leave the area. Ambassador Hill explained to us that this it was an urgent consultation that needed to be made face to face between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milosevic, and that he had to fly with Mr. Sainovic in the hope that things would be moving on the Belgrade side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked about the letter to Mrs. Albright that you and your delegation wrote. I think it's at page 49, line 19, of today's transcript. You began one of your answers to Mr. O'Sullivan by saying, "I will tell you the details because it's quite important," but he stopped you at that point. He wanted just a simple answer to his question. Did you get to tell us all the details you wanted to about the drafting of that letter to Mrs. Albright on the 23rd of February?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, we were in a situation in which our delegation could not make up its mind about what to do with the document, and Mr. Hill, Ambassador Hill, came and the mediators, Majorski and Petritsch, came to our room to ask for our final decision on this. And then we were giving the response, or I should clarify, it was Ambassador Hill himself and his aides coming, and then asked whether we had made a decision on this. And this was basically a "yes" or a "no" situation. It was nothing to be explained further. And the way the four principal -- the three principals were explaining the issue, it came as if our delegation was refusing. We were deliberating on this issue up to that moment. And the main obstacle -- the main obstacles were, of course, the referendum issue, which we touched on, and the question of the KLA. And there was a minority but a vociferous minority that was against this agreement. And I thought that what we could formulate is our -- where we have things in common. And the things in common were that we were not against most of this agreement; that, in principle, we would go with it, especially since it guaranteed a degree of security with NATO, international presence, and a political process that would then lead towards a referendum, or what we thought was going to be a referendum. Therefore, I submitted a formula -- a formulation by which we recognised that we would accept this document. We needed a period of consultation with our people. It was clear that many people who had fought this war, the KLA were having their doubts about this agreement, and that we needed to go and explain back home what it meant, and what all these particularities and all these dilemmas would produce in the future. And as suggested, we would send this to -- not as suggested, but we would send this to the contact group, and at the same time we would use the opportunity to address Secretary Albright on an issue which we thought had been taken away from us, which was this letter on the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] And that formulation was then adopted unanimously by the whole delegation. And I signed that statement and sent it to the contact group as a sign of our approval of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The last topic I want to ask you about: Mr. Fila showed you some documents in connection with the education agreement and steps towards implementing that. Exhibit 2D2 were the minutes of a meeting on the 6th of August, 1998. That was the document that showed that European Commission was going to contribute something in the neighbourhood of 4 million, regarding the construction of student pavilions of the new technical faculty, et cetera. To your knowledge, were any of those construction projects undertaken or completed before the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] They had -- the whole technical faculty was destroyed, especially on the day of the handover. When the Serb authorities handed over the technical faculty, a lot of it was destroyed, and there were disgruntled Serb students who were doing the destruction, up to the point at which the Serb police had to intervene. There might have been, but I don't think that was the focus of the attention. As I say, at the time when all of this was signed and being thought to be implemented, we already had a major refugee crisis being developed both in western Kosova and in central Kosova, where the fighting erupted. We had such a big crisis that Ambassador Hill had to call, in my presence, in May, Sadako Ogata, on a Sunday, to actually see what the UNHCR could do about 5.000 refugees that were in the Decani area where there was still snow, and they were going to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. I did want to tender Exhibit 715, which was the San Egidio education agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, you did say that there were two or three colleges opened following this agreement, and you referred to them being part of the technical faculty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. The technical faculty was the first faculty under this agreement to be returned. May I remind you, it's two years after the agreement has been signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that. But the question Mr. Hannis just asked was whether, prior to March 1999, any work had actually been done following the implementation agreement in 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. The Albanological Institute was handed over to the people at the institute. This was the first building to be handed over, to be returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But was any of the EU money spent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that completes your evidence, Mr. Surroi. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it. We will take account of all that you've said today, along with the statement that you gave before, plus the transcript of the evidence you gave on the previous occasion. It will all assist us towards our final deliberations in the matter. So thank you very much again, and you're free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The most recent word I have, Your Honour, is we have not located Mr. Dashi. We were checking at the hotel and apparently he is not in his room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm kicking myself for not telling him yesterday to come back today. I thought -- there is always this feeling in your mind that it might just turn out differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had thought this witness would take the entire day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do you want more time to try to deal with this or is it a lost cause?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I really have no idea whether he's going to come back or -- since he may have gone to visit friends. I have no idea, Your Honour. I mean, we could take a short break and I can advise the Court in 20 minutes whether we've located him. But I think maybe it's better if we just start fresh in the morning with him. In addition, I had indicated to the Court that another witness we had scheduled for this week we will not be calling this week. That was Witness K80. So we will resume with Mr. Dashi, and the witness after him will be K25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just remind me, Mr. Hannis. We will have K25?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then K24 and then Mr. Sweeny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that will fill the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all we currently have. We are trying to see if we can get somebody else in the event that those don't fill out the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We certainly won't continue today now. But can I make one serious point about timekeeping?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's great to finish sharper than you expect, but because of the potential that this case has for extending, depending on the length of the Defence cases, for a considerable period beyond the conclusion of the Prosecution case, it is fairly important, I think, to do things as efficiently as we can at the moment; and if, on reassessing the situation, you see the possibility of spare time this week - I'm not referring to today, I'm referring to later in the week, obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- then perhaps you can try and address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will make efforts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. So we will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.21 p.m.,
